newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. sees progress to global telecom pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees progress to global telecom pact.

text.p: A senior U.S. official said on Monday he saw progress towards agreement on a global pact opening up the $600 billion market in basic telecommunications by the deadline at the end of this week.

But the official, Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang, said although more countries were making market opening offers, including key emerging economies in Asia, or improving packages already tabled, important issues remained to be solved.

"We are making progress. However, we're not there yet," Lang told reporters. "But we still have some problems that have to be worked out in order for this thing to be successful.... There is going to have to be further improvement in offers."

Lang spoke after a meeting of the telecoms negotiating group in the World Trade Organisation (WTO), at which Malaysia, a key hold-out, formally tabled its first offer, together with two other developing countries -- Ghana and Grenada.

At the session, WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero appealed to negotiators and their governments to recognise the importance of a pact, which he said was vital to the success of the two-year-old WTO.

Lang's assessment is important as the United States is the world's biggest telecoms market and last April derailed talks on a deal, when it walked away arguing that there was not a "critical mass" of good offers on the table.

Asked for his view on whether this level had yet been achieved in the latest effort, which has a deadline of February 15 for completion, Lang said: "We'll just have to make a judgment (later) about critical mass.
"Today, we don't have it, but we're getting closer."

Earlier, a key trade diplomat said the chances of a deal "depend entirely on the U.S." He added: "Much of this exercise is about making Washington happy that there is enough to make a opening its own market to all-comers worthwhile."

Lang made clear Washington was unhappy with the level of opening to foreign ownership of telecoms companies offered by Canada, whose proposal allows a maximum of 47.8 per cent of equity capital to be held by non-Canadians, by Mexico and South Korea.

Talks were continuing with Canada, and also with the European Union -- whose offer tabled last November has been criticised by U.S. officials for apparently seeking to exclude provision of video services.
But Lang declined to give details on this. "I don't think it would be helpful at this stage," he said.
Earlier, a senior EU negotiator insisted that complaints from Washington -- and concern voiced by international news agencies -- over the video issue were based on a misunderstanding.

EU officials say they believe they can convince their key partners that commitments to allow such services are covered by other global agreements under the WTO's overall accord on trade in services, GATS, and were not essential in its telcoms offer.

With the latest three offers, a total of 57 countries including all 14 member states of the EU have packages on the table, accounting for what WTO analysts say is over 91 per cent of the global market.
